title: Concussion: assessment and a gradual return to daily life
intro: Concussion is a brain injury caused by a blow or sudden jolt to the head or body. You do not have to lose consciousness to have one. Symptoms can develop later, and a seemingly minor injury can coexist with a more dangerous problem. Stop the activity and seek medical advice when concussion is suspected; this article cannot rule out bleeding or a neck injury.

sections.heading: Recognise changes, including delayed ones
paragraphs: Headache, dizziness, nausea, poor balance and sensitivity to light or noise can occur. Thinking may feel slow or foggy, with difficulty concentrating or remembering the event. Sleep, mood and behaviour may change. In a young child, reduced feeding, unusual crying or loss of interest in play may be more noticeable than a description of headache. Tell the clinician how the injury happened, any loss of consciousness or memory, previous concussions and all medicines. Blood-thinning medicines or a bleeding disorder make prompt advice particularly important even after an apparently small injury.

sections.heading: Danger signs need emergency help
paragraphs: Call emergency services for inability to wake or stay awake, a seizure, new weakness or numbness, slurred speech, worsening confusion, repeated vomiting, a worsening severe headache, unequal pupils or double vision. Clear fluid or bleeding from an ear after injury, an obvious skull injury or a high-energy accident also needs emergency assessment. An inconsolable child or one who will not feed needs urgent attention. Avoid unnecessary movement when neck injury is possible and follow the dispatcher's instructions. Do not let an injured person drive themselves. New danger signs matter even after an earlier reassuring examination.

sections.heading: Examination and observation answer different questions
paragraphs: A clinician assesses neurological function, symptoms and risk factors to decide whether observation or imaging is needed. A brain CT may look for bleeding or a fracture; it is not necessary for every concussion. A normal scan does not exclude concussion, which often causes no visible structural change on routine imaging. If home care is appropriate, obtain written instructions and make sure a responsible adult can stay for at least the first day. Clarify what to monitor and whom to call. Sleep is normally allowed after assessment; difficulty waking is a danger sign, not a reason to force everyone to stay awake all night.

sections.heading: Relative rest, then manageable activity
paragraphs: A short period of relative rest, commonly the first day or two, can help. Prolonged complete bed rest or sitting in a dark room all day is not the usual recovery plan. Then build up gentle activity such as a short walk and simple daily tasks according to medical advice. Reduce an activity if it clearly worsens symptoms. Temporarily limit demanding screen use or noisy environments if they provoke symptoms, and keep regular sleep. Avoid alcohol, recreational drugs and unapproved sleeping medicines. Ask which pain medicines are suitable. Driving, machinery and work at height need particular caution while concentration or balance is affected.

sections.heading: School, work and sport need different plans
paragraphs: A child can often return to school early with rest breaks, reduced workload and extra time, rather than waiting for every mild symptom to disappear. Adults may need shorter work periods or altered duties. Return to sport requires a supervised gradual progression and clinical clearance; someone with suspected concussion must not return to play the same day. Avoid activities risking another head impact during recovery. Most people improve over days to weeks, but persistent symptoms are real and may need targeted rehabilitation. Arrange follow-up if recovery stalls, symptoms worsen with return to activity or problems remain beyond a few weeks; do not simply push through them.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: no blackout does not mean no concussion
examples.text: After a collision, a football player remains awake but feels dizzy and cannot remember the previous play. The coach removes her from the match and arranges assessment. Feeling better later that afternoon does not allow her to return that day.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: adjusting a school day
examples.text: After medical assessment, a pupil returns with shorter lessons and quiet breaks. Reading for a long stretch brings on headache, so the family and school shorten those periods and update the clinician. A new episode of repeated vomiting would instead trigger urgent reassessment.
